newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: FEATURE - In Afghanistan, little hope for shell-shocked.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - In Afghanistan, little hope for shell-shocked.

text.p: The only indications this war-torn building is an Afghan mental hospital are a patient's couch on the otherwise bare third floor and two inmates sitting outside in the late afternoon sun, both twitching involuntarily.
There are no facilities, little medicine and even less food: last night the few remaining patients had only bread to eat.
Each floor is empty save a few scattered chairs, shards of glass for windows and, in the consulting room, a wispy see-through curtain to shield the patient's couch.

A country like Afghanistan, which has suffered varying degrees of war for nearly two decades and shows no sign of achieving peace, is a fertile breeding ground for mental illnesses well beyond this hospital's capacity to cope.

"Now everybody (in Afghanistan) is suffering from mental or psychological problems. Before we had up to 50 or 60 people coming for treatment every week. I have no figures, but everyone is suffering," resident doctor Timur Shah says in an interview.

Traumas from looting, destruction, killing, war and its fallout have affected everyone, he says. Patients range from fighters suffering from shell-shock to widows who cannot cope with the daily struggle of surviving alone.
Few seek treatment until the condition is serious.
"Afghanistan is not like western countries. To have mildly suffering patients come for treatment doesn't happen here. Normally they are critical when they come," he says.

A case in point: Amin, a dark, thickly bearded man who says he is either 28 or 30 years old, lost all his family in fighting some time ago, and while his handshake is firm he eyes wander and he plays incessantly with a large blue ring.

"I came voluntarily because I would get nervous and hysterical so I would sometimes fight people," he says as he sits cross-legged on a metal bed covered with a single blanket and filthy pillow. It is his second spell here.

For Amin and the few other patients remaining -- most have left because there is not enough food -- the chances of proper care are slim. Shah says he is not a specialist in mental health and can do little for them besides give medication.
Funding, already sparse, will be cut further under the capital's month-old Taleban administration, the doctors in charge of the hospital have been told.
Aid is not enough: yesterday's supply of medicines from a French agency was enough for only one day.

Worse, perhaps, is a faint, photocopied notice pinned to a door. This lists the new hospital rules under the Islamic Taleban, who have banned women in areas under control from most public roles or education.
According to the document, posted in mid-October, most communication is banned between the sexes, including doctors with other doctors and doctors and patients.

In a hospital -- Afghanistan's only such institution, apart from a private clinic and an asylum for advanced cases -- that had only female psychologists and counted on group therapy sessions, this is a disaster.
No new women patients have been accepted, and all female patients have been sent home. Only three doctors can be found to work night duty.
The female ward is locked and empty, the only visible concession to comfort a faded pink curtain flapping in the breeze.

Now the hospital is down to four patients, including Amin, and a young, shaven-headed drug addict who identifies himself as Zaban-i-Allah -- Tongue of God -- and within the space of a sentence turns from hospitable to hostile.
"Thank you speaking good English yes, sit down, good. Go. Go!" he says, his voice moving from quiet to a hiss.

For 27-year old Shah, who graduated from the Kabul Institute last year, it is a difficult choice. Sitting on a bed on the top floor reading Western medical texts to improve his English, he is far away from his dream of general practice.
"If I had more facilities I would continue my work with these patients," he says, gesturing at his office, devoid of any equipment except an ageing typewriter under a nearby bed.
Outside, in a clear blue sky, a jet fighter can be heard flying over the capital. It is probably Taleban but no one can be sure.
"Nobody cares about this place," shrugs Shah.
